story.card_text: On April 29, 1852, the night after Boston switched on its fire alarm telegraph, the first real alarm came in. The 1889 department history says it was given 'from District 1, Station 7, now Box 12, located at that time on the Cooper-street Church,' for a fire in John Ward's building at Causeway and Charlestown Streets, a few blocks west of here. A 2020 Globe story names the man who sent it, J.H. Goodale, and calls the box 1212 - the number the City's file gives the box on this corner. A hundred and sixty-six years later, early on December 28, 2018, with 911 down, a resident pulled the box at Cooper and Endicott for a fire on Endicott Street. Firefighters knocked it down and nobody was hurt. Whether today's 1212 stands where the 1852 church station did is unproven: nobody has yet matched the church to a period map. Alarm Club lists the first-alarm box as Wanted.

story.card_text: Boston's alarm office has moved three times: from Court Square in 1852, to the top of City Hall on School Street in 1865, to 60 Bristol Street in the South End in 1895, and here. The cornerstone went down in July 1924, the building was dedicated in September 1925, and the office opened at 8:00 a.m. on December 27, 1925. Two minutes later it took its first alarm, from Box 2328 on Westland Avenue. Richard Shaw of O'Connell & Shaw designed it in Indiana limestone, Italian Renaissance style, and it took a special act of the Legislature to build it on state-controlled parkland. The front explains itself: built 'to fortify and extend the principle of organized resistance to the scourge of fire.' The IEEE's own listing says its 2004 Milestone plaque for the 1852 system 'can be viewed' here; the fire historians put it on School Street. And the number the historians list for this office, '12-1591', matches a box the City's file puts at Boylston and the Fenway - one of three the department says have been removed.

story.narration_script: This limestone building on the Fens is the Boston Fire Alarm Office. Every street box you read today reports here. The office started in eighteen fifty-two at Court Square, moved to the top of City Hall on School Street, then to Bristol Street in the South End, and finally here. It opened at eight in the morning on December twenty-seventh, nineteen twenty-five. Two minutes later it took its first alarm, from a box on Westland Avenue. It took a special act of the state legislature to put it on park land. Look at the front. It says it was built to fortify and extend the principle of organized resistance to the scourge of fire. The engineers' society that honored the eighteen fifty-two system says its plaque can be seen here. The fire historians say it's on School Street. Nobody has settled that yet. Stay on the path. This is a working dispatch center.

pitch_60: On November ninth, eighteen seventy-two, a Boston police officer heard boys yelling fire and figured they were teasing him. Then he saw the flames. He had the key to the alarm box in his pocket. The alarm still went in a quarter of an hour late, seven hundred seventy-six buildings burned, and nobody has fully explained why it was late. The Eighteen Fifty-Two Hunt walks the world's first municipal fire alarm telegraph, switched on in Boston in eighteen fifty-two. Thirteen stops through Downtown Crossing, the Financial District and Fort Point. Each riddle walks you to a corner, and almost every answer is the number on a real red box, read from the sidewalk. Then you get the story: the cranks people turned according to how excited they were, the week the horses were sick, the wet carpets a witness said stopped the fire, and the night nine one one went down and a box still worked. Don't pull anything. Just read it. It starts at Government Center. Give it about two hours.

seo.landing_copy:
Boston's red fire alarm boxes aren't decoration. In 1852 this city switched on the world's first municipal fire alarm telegraph, and the network those boxes belong to has been running ever since - on its own wires, separate from the phones. When 911 went down in December 2018, a North End resident reported a fire by pulling one.

The 1852 Hunt is a free, self-guided walk through that network and the fires around it. It starts at Government Center, a block from where the first alarm office worked, and runs through Downtown Crossing to the corner where the Great Fire of 1872 began. You'll stand where its first alarm went in - about a quarter of an hour late - and find out why the usual story about a missing key doesn't match the inquiry's own testimony - the officer who opened the box had his key in his pocket - and why the real cause is still an open question. Then on to the spot where the fire was stopped, the square it created, a firehouse built into a skyscraper, and an old double-company firehouse in Fort Point.

It's thirteen stops, about two hours and three kilometers, flat and step-free. Each stop is a riddle that walks you to the next corner, and the answer is something you can only get by looking: usually the number on a real alarm box, read from the sidewalk. Then you get the story, with its sources.

Every fact comes from a primary record or a named source - the 1873 commission report on the Great Fire, the 1889 fire department history, the Boston Fire Historical Society, the City's own box data - and every source is listed. Where the sources disagree, we say so.

The 1852 Hunt is one of two free walks in Off the Bricks: Boston Hunts, made with Alarm Club, the game where Bostonians check the City's fire alarm box list on foot. Neither is affiliated with the City of Boston or the Boston Fire Department. Never touch, open or stick anything on a box. Read it and move on.

Free. No account. Start at Government Center.

story.card_text: Before Boston's fire alarm telegraph took a single real alarm, it rang the city's bells from New York. The 1889 department history says the idea was first written off as 'a visionary or "cranky" scheme,' until Mayor Josiah Quincy pushed the council to look into it. Moses Farmer built bell-striking machines, one hung in the old City Hall belfry and wired to New York, and an operator there rang Boston's bells - which, the history says, 'caused a false alarm of fire.' The city put up $10,000 for 'an experiment, being without precedent in the world,' and at noon on April 28, 1852, switched on the world's first municipal fire alarm telegraph. It ran from an office in the City Building at Court Square and Williams Court - the lane people now call Pi Alley, just past Old City Hall. The first real alarm came the next night, April 29, at 8:25. In December 1865 the office moved about a hundred feet, to the top of the new City Hall at 45 School Street, where the 1889 history puts it 'in the dome.' It stayed until 1895, and has been at 59 Fenway since 1925.

story.look_now: Look down School Street to Old City Hall's mansard roof - the alarm office worked under it from 1865 to 1895.
story.narration_script: Stand at the top of School Street and look down the hill. Before Boston's fire alarm telegraph took a single real alarm, it rang the city's bells from New York. People had called the idea cranky. Then the inventors hung a bell-striking machine in the old City Hall belfry and wired it to New York. An operator there tapped his key, and Boston's bells rang. The papers called it a false alarm of fire. The city paid ten thousand dollars for an experiment without precedent in the world, and at noon on April twenty-eighth, eighteen fifty-two, it switched on the world's first municipal fire alarm telegraph. It ran from an office at Court Square, in the little lane people now call Pi Alley, just past Old City Hall. The first real alarm came the next night, April twenty-ninth, at eight twenty-five. In eighteen sixty-five the office moved up into the dome of the new City Hall, right there on School Street, and stayed until eighteen ninety-five.

story.card_text: For the first thirty years you could not just pull a Boston fire alarm. The boxes were locked. Keys went to what the Boston Fire Historical Society calls 'trusted citizens in the area'; everyone else had to find a keyholder first. An 1855 ordinance put a committee in charge of who was 'intrusted with the care of the keys of the signal-boxes,' and fined false alarms two to fifty dollars. It didn't hold - the 1889 department history says every lock was later changed 'on account of the keys being held by irresponsible people and frequent false alarms.' This corner has been in the paperwork a long time. The Great Fire inquiry of 1872 mentions 'Box 42, on Winter street.' And a history of the system by Joe Maurath records the first keyless door, a T-handle, going onto Box 42 at Tremont and Winter on April 16, 1881. Two weeks later the boxes were ordered painted red. Until then they were black. The last locked box in Boston was gone by October 1907. Today's box here carries four digits - your answer.

story.look_now: Look at the door on the box in front of you - nobody needs a key to raise an alarm on it. That started here. Look, don't touch.
story.narration_script: You're at Tremont and Winter. For the first thirty years, you could not just pull a fire alarm in Boston. The boxes were locked. Keys went to trusted people in the neighborhood. Everyone else had to find a keyholder first. An eighteen fifty-five city ordinance fined false alarms anywhere from two to fifty dollars. It didn't help much. The old department history says every lock had to be changed because keys were held by irresponsible people. The box on this street had a number, forty-two, as far back as the Great Fire of eighteen seventy-two. And according to one history of the system, on April sixteenth, eighteen eighty-one, Box forty-two, right here, got the first keyless door in the city. Two weeks later the boxes were ordered painted red. Before that, they were black. By October of nineteen-oh-seven, every box in the city had a keyless door.

story.card_text: On November 10, after burning out of control for more than twelve hours, the fire was stopped at the corner of Washington and Milk - just up the block. The people in the buildings on the west side of Washington Street climbed up and kept their eaves wet with carpets and cloths, and one witness said 'these carpets and old rugs stopped the fire from crossing.' And the postmaster, William L. Burt, who pushed that night for blowing up buildings in the fire's path, testified: 'Persons came to me three times and desired to blow up the Old South Church. I told them, "There is no necessity for it; we can stop the fire there."' Old South, where the Tea Party meeting was held in 1773, is still standing.

Here's the version you'll hear on tours. One engine from Portsmouth, New Hampshire, called the Kearsarge, saved the building by itself. The people across Washington Street climbed up on their buildings with wet carpets, and one witness said the carpets and old rugs stopped the fire from crossing. story.card_text: Every address in Boston is cross-referenced to a fire alarm box, a bit like a zip code - that's how Michael Gerry of the Boston Fire Museum explained it to WBUR in 2018. When a call comes in, the dispatch voice names the nearest box, and the companies follow their route to it. The boxes are the city's fire map. Their names have always been code. In 1852, the 1889 department history explains, a box was a rhythm on the bells: three dots, a pause, then a dash and three dots meant district three, station six. The first real alarm, at 8:25 on the night of April 29, 1852, came 'from District 1, Station 7, now Box 12, located at that time on the Cooper-street Church' in the North End, for a fire at Causeway and Charlestown Streets. A 2020 Globe story names the man who sent it, J.H. Goodale, and calls it Box 1212 - the number the City's file gives the box at Cooper and Endicott today. So one box has had at least three names, and whether today's 1212 stands where the church station did is still open; Alarm Club lists it as Wanted. In the City's file, the boxes around Post Office Square all start with 12.

subtitle: Boston's fire alarm telegraph, read off the boxes
summary: In 1852 Boston switched on the world's first municipal fire alarm telegraph. Twenty years later its alarm for the Great Fire went in a quarter of an hour late, and nobody has fully explained why. This walk follows the network from School Street through the ground the fire burned to Post Office Square and Fort Point, and most answers are numbers you read off real boxes, from the sidewalk.
